Understanding the Pink Gene (CAL / HPS3)

The "Pink" French Bulldog is one of the most unique and sought-after color variations in the breed today. This phenotype is governed by the HPS3 gene, commonly referred to in the breeding community as the CAL gene (Coat Color and Light). Unlike standard colors, Pink provides a distinct rosy, translucent glow to the skin and coat.

The Genetics: n/A vs. A/A

The Pink gene is autosomal recessive. This means a dog must inherit the mutation from both parents to express the physical "Pink" characteristics. Using the nomenclature provided by labs like Animal Genetics, the results are broken down as follows:

  • n/n: The dog is negative for the Pink mutation and cannot pass it to offspring.
  • n/A (Carrier): The dog carries one copy of the Pink gene. The dog will appear as a standard color but can pass the gene to 50% of its puppies.
  • A/A (Full Pink): The dog has two copies of the Pink mutation and will visually express the Pink phenotype.

Physical Characteristics

A "Full Pink" Frenchie (A/A) is easily distinguished by its lack of heavy surface melanin. Key traits include:

  • The "Rosy" Glow: A soft, peach-to-pink hue on the skin, most visible around the muzzle, eyes, and paw pads.
  • Lighter Pigmentation: Even on dogs that would otherwise be dark, the Pink gene dilutes the pigment, often resulting in a "warm" or "shimmering" coat.
  • Eye Color: Pink Frenchies often possess lighter eye colors, ranging from golden amber to soft aqua tones.

Pink vs. Cream (The Masking Effect)

It is a common misconception that Pink and Cream are the same. While both can result in a light-colored dog, they are genetically distinct. Cream (the e-locus) is epistatic, meaning it can "hide" the Pink gene. A dog can be genetically A/A but appear to be a standard Cream. DNA testing is the only way to confirm the presence of the HPS3 mutation.

Breeder's Note: The Pink gene is not a form of Albinism. It is a specific pigment transport mutation (HPS3) that creates a beautiful, healthy dilution without the health risks associated with true albino traits.

definition: Also known as 'Domino'. An ancestral variant of the E-locus that creates a textured, two-toned gradient on each hair strand.

Understanding the eA Gene: The "Husky" Domino

The eA allele (Ancient Domino) is part of the E-Locus series. While it has existed in dogs for thousands of years, it has recently become a sensation in French Bulldogs due to its ability to create a "Husky-like" appearance. This gene works by reducing the production of dark pigment (eumelanin), allowing the lighter base colors to "creep" up the body.

The "Visual Domino" (eA/e)

In French Bulldogs, the eA gene is most dramatic when paired with a copy of recessive cream. Breeders typically refer to a dog as a "Visual eA Husky" when the genotype is eA/e. The presence of the single 'e' copy clears the coat just enough to make the Domino patterns "pop."

Key Visual Indicators

  • The Widow’s Peak: One of the most iconic traits of a Domino Frenchie is a clear, pointed "peak" of darker hair on the forehead that mimics the look of a Siberian Husky.
  • Facial Mask Reduction: Even if a dog is genetically Em (Melanistic Mask), the eA gene can shrink or completely remove the black mask, often leaving "goggles" around the eyes.
  • Hair Strand Gradients: Unlike standard colors where a hair is one solid shade, Domino hairs are often bi-colored or "banded." The base of the hair is usually much lighter, while the tip retains the darker pigment.
  • The Gradient Effect: The dog will often show a "wrap-around" effect where the color is darkest on the spine and fades into a pale or white underbelly, chest, and legs.

Genetic Combinations

The eA gene interacts differently depending on its partner at the E-Locus:

  • eA/eA: A "Double Domino." These dogs are typically very light, often appearing almost like a cream but with "ghost" patterns of their base color (Blue, Cocoa, etc.).
  • eA/e: The preferred "Visual Husky" look. This provides the best contrast for the widow's peak and body gradients.
  • E/eA: The dog may show a slight "creeping" of tan or a small widow's peak, but the standard dominant black (E) usually hides the most dramatic Domino effects.
Webmaster Note: Because the eA gene affects how Tan Points (at) are expressed, it can actually make a "Trindle" dog look like a clean "Tan Point" by suppressing the visible brindle stripping!

definition: The 'Teddy Bear' phenotype. Requires two copies of the Fluffy gene (L/L) combined with at least one copy of Furnishings.
moreInfo:
The Floodle (or 'Visual Teddy Bear') is a precise architectural intersection of two distinct genetic markers: FGF5 (The L-Locus) and RSPO2 (Furnishings).

The RSPO2 Dominance

Unlike the Fluffy gene, which is recessive, Furnishings (F) is a dominant trait. This means a dog only needs one copy (n/F) to display the phenotype. Even in short-haired dogs, one copy of the F-gene creates the 'Wire-hair' texture and facial 'furniture' (mustache and eyebrows).

The 'Producer' vs. The 'Visual'

  • The Teddy Bear Producer (Sh/L + n/F): This dog carries one copy of the Fluffy gene. Visually, they often appear as 'Wire-hair' or 'Scruffy' textures. They are elite assets for programs looking to 'unlock' the Floodle look in the next generation.
  • The Visual Floodle (L/L + n/F): The 'Gold Standard' aesthetic. This is achieved when two copies of the Fluffy gene (Length) are paired with the dominant Furnishings gene (Architecture).

The Science of Texture

In a true Floodle, the FGF5 gene provides the coat length, while the RSPO2 gene provides the 'lift' and wave. Without the furnishing gene, a long-haired dog is simply a 'Fluffy' with hair that lays flat and lacks the signature teddy-bear facial structure.

Note: Because this coat is more complex than standard DNA, it requires the OKC Omega Mania protocol to maintain fiber elasticity and prevent breakage.

RSPO2: The Science of Furnishings

In the world of canine genetics, the RSPO2 gene is the primary architect of coat texture. While other genes determine length or color, RSPO2 determines the growth pattern—specifically the presence of facial hair (mustaches, eyebrows, and beards) and a specialized wiry coat texture.

The n/F Marker: Dominance Defined

Most genetic laboratories, such as Animal Genetics, mark a dog carrying this gene as n/F. It is critical to understand that unlike the 'Fluffy' gene (FGF5), Furnishings is a Dominant trait.

  • n/n (Negative): The dog has a standard smooth coat and will never produce furnishings unless bred to an 'F' carrier.
  • n/F (Carrier/Visual): Because the gene is dominant, a dog with only one copy will display facial furniture and a textured coat.
  • F/F (Double Copy): The dog is 'Homozygous' for furnishings and will pass the trait to 100% of its offspring, regardless of the mate.

The 'Hidden' Asset: Short-Haired Furnishings

A dog can be n/F and still have a short coat (Sh/Sh or Sh/L). In these cases, the dog often displays a 'Wire-hair' or 'Scruffy' look. While they aren't 'Floodles' themselves, these are the Elite Producers of the program. When an n/F dog is bred to a Fluffy (L/L), you unlock the architectural 'Teddy Bear' facial structure in the offspring.

Maintenance of the 'F' Fiber

The furnishings gene changes the physical structure of the hair shaft, making it more porous. To prevent the 'brittle' texture often found in lower-quality wire-coats, our Raw & Paw Protocol emphasizes Omega Mania and Goat Brew to provide the biotin and essential fatty acids needed to keep the furniture soft, elastic, and high-definition.
